- **Items:** 10 plus a bonus, each a thing not to buy with the better buy. Shortest: item 2, smartwatches (101 words, about 0:55); longest: item 7, trend pieces (171 words, about 1:25). Typical: 110 to 145 words, about 1:00. The order is loose: two viral objects first (the tumbler, the smartwatch), then skin care (which hosts the sponsor), then luxury, sales and trends (the three mindset items), then household items, ending on hair tools as a bonus. Item one starts at 0:27, word 79.
- **Item shape:** the thing named in a fixed frame ("the next thing ... never buy is") → the French reason (culture, walking, small homes, old buildings) → the better buy ("instead, French women prefer") → sometimes a rule (80/20, wait for a trend to become timeless). No try-on of the bad thing; no check step; no result said in look words.
- **The title's promise:** "10 Things" said at 0:21 and in the close (13:50); paid with ten plus a bonus. "French Women Never Buy" is the fixed frame of every item. "(But Everyone Else Does)" is never said; the contrast is implied (abroad, "here in France", American bathrooms at 13:12). The promise is paid, but about half the items are not clothing (tumbler, smartwatch, mini fridge, smart-home gadgets, subscription boxes).
- **Feelings:** 1 of 11 items names an inner feeling about the viewer: item 7, regret after buying a trend (before the swap, "you"). Items 4, 9 and 10 use "feels" about the purchase (excessive, thoughtful), not about the woman.
- **Villain:** overconsumption and viral, trendy or display buying (said at 0:09, 11:09); brands are named as examples, not attacked. Aimed at habits; no person blamed. The implied other side is "everyone else" (Americans), never named as a villain.
- **Hard words:** none of frumpy, old lady, granny or dated. "Waste of money" and "excessive" are the hard words, said of purchases.
- **CTA placement:** the sponsor read, 3:18-5:18 (289 words, about 2:00), inside item 3 and framed as her own better buy, with a link and offer. At the end, two comment asks (13:54, 14:20), a subscribe and social-media ask (14:22). 
- **Ending:** a short close on the ten things, a comment ask, then a repeat of her own spending habits (mid-range and drugstore), a second comment ask, subscribe, follow and goodbye. No recap of the items.
- **How the national lens is stated (the French-lens model):** claims about French women are mostly flat statements ("French women never buy", "it's simply not in our culture"), voiced from inside ("we", "us", "here in Paris"), and often backed by a practical reason (walking, small bags, small bathrooms, thick walls, products stable at room temperature). Hedges are frequent inside the items ("usually" 7 times, "rarely", "at least, it's not really in our culture", "simply less common here"), so the title's "never" is softened in speech without saying so. The comparison side is mostly unstated.
- **What sets it apart from other models of its type:**
  - Every "never" comes with a reason the viewer can check against her own life (walking, small homes, old walls), so the lens reads as practical sense rather than snobbery.
  - The mindset items (sales, trends, display luxury) give portable rules: a discount doesn't make it worth having; 80/20; wait for a trend to prove itself.
  - Permission is built in for the viewer who still likes trends (9:28), so the rule doesn't shame her.

- **Arc:** insider pride (we don't shop like that) → the reason, item by item → the better, calmer buy → permission to keep a little trend → intentional and unhurried.

## Why it works

The comments show the video's real pull: viewers recognise themselves in the French habits. "I just realized I am French :) at least in spirit." (323 likes); "I am more French than I thought!" (175 likes). The pushback is practical and about the US: "I like to have water with me. I don't drink coffee." (96 likes); "carrying water is an essential part whee I live in Arizona" (87 likes); "going to a Salon twice a week is way more money than expensive hair tools" (59 likes); and against the lens itself: "it's not just French women who stand apart" (127 likes). One viewer had already made the swap: "The aftercare supplied by my dermatologist was Avene which I now use." (53 likes). The pace is slow and deliberate (about 128 words a minute), the first item lands at 0:27 after a 78-word hook, and the fixed item frame makes the list easy to follow; the sponsor read sits in item 3 for two minutes and draws one dry comment.
